name: French Grey
lede: French grey is a pale, almost neutral grey that English first met as a naturalist's term: Patrick Syme put it on his 1814 color chart, and a young Charles Darwin used it for an octopus.

sections.title: A grey that leans every way
sections.body:
*French grey* is a pale, nearly neutral grey, and the books do not agree on which way it leans. Paterson's dictionary calls it a bluish grey [7], St Clair's glossary a very pale grey-green [8], and the chart that introduced the name describes it as a whitish grey touched faintly by black and by carmine [2]. The swatch here sits close to neutral, at a chroma of about 6 and a hue angle of 110 degrees, a hair toward yellow-green [9].

Modern systems keep it in nearly the same place. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files it in block 154, Ridgway's 1912 atlas gives it a plate with a slightly darker swatch, and the German RAL range has a near twin in 7044 Silk Grey, less than one unit away in CIEDE2000 [9]. Its closest relatives among the chart greys are [[pearl-grey]] and [[steel-grey]], and the color word it keeps company with most often in paintings is [[ash]] [9][10].

sections.title: Syme's chart
sections.body:
The name entered English science through a book of color samples [3]. Patrick Syme, trained as a botanist and entomologist, took the small mineral vocabulary of Abraham Werner and widened it into a standard for animals, plants and rocks alike [3]. His first edition appeared in 1814 with 108 colors, and the second, in 1821, ran to 110 [3][12].

Syme described French grey as Werner's steel grey with the metallic lustre taken away [2]. His natural example was the breast of the pied wagtail, and it is the only one he gave [1]. Compare [[pearl-grey]], which he illustrated with a gull's back, a flower petal and a stone [1].

Where the term came from is a small disagreement inside one book. Baty's chart pages list French grey as one of Syme's own additions among greys borrowed from Werner, Picardet and Lenz [1]. Her discussion of his vocabulary says instead that some terms, French grey among them, were already common English and that Syme only popularized them [3]. Why it is *French* is undocumented in the books we read [3][7]. Paterson lists a whole run of French colors: beige, berry, blue, green, grey, navy, ochre, pink, purple and ultramarine [7]. Only French purple has a known story, a lichen dye of the 1850s that helped turn [[mauve]] from a dye's name into a color's [7].

sections.title: A grey on the Beagle
sections.body:
Syme's chart traveled. In September 1831, while preparing for the *Beagle* voyage, Charles Darwin asked his mentor John Henslow to keep Syme's colors in mind, and a copy of the 1821 edition went into the ship's library [5]. On 28 January 1832, at the Cape Verde Islands, Darwin met an octopus and, as Baty tells it, was jolted into remembering that colors had to be recorded on the spot [5].

His note describes an animal whose general color was French grey with many spots of bright yellow, crossed by clouds that ran from hyacinth red to chestnut brown [5]. Baty observes that every one of those terms comes straight from Syme, and [[hyacinth-red]] is on the same chart [5]. Finlay quotes what appears to be the same episode and adds that the animal looked brownish purple in deep water and yellowish green in the shallows, "or rather French gray" [6].

The practical problem was spoilage. Sea animals lose their colors the moment they leave the water, so a naturalist on a rolling deck juggled the animal, the chart and the notebook before the color faded [5].

sections.title: From botany to birds
sections.body:
Botanists took the term up quickly. Baty offers the *Botanical Register*, edited by Sydenham Edwards and John Lindley, as the example of English-speaking botanists adopting Syme's names, with French grey among them [4]. The American botanist William Barton, who wanted to print Syme's samples in his *Flora of North America*, could manage only a black-and-white copy in 1823 [4]. Baty reads his complaint as a sign that he missed the chart's point, which was standard names, not recipes for mixing paint [4].

The line ran on to ornithology. Robert Ridgway's *Nomenclature of Colors for Naturalists* of 1886 contained at least 19 of Syme's terms, and his *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* of 1912 laid out 1,115 colors on 53 plates [13]. French grey appears in both Ridgway books in our library [9]. Maerz and Paul's dictionary of 1930 gives 1814 as the year it was first recorded, which matches Syme's first edition [9][12].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 2,120 works, about 9 per cent [10]. It is a pale color, and in 94 per cent of those paintings it is among the lightest colors on the canvas [10]. Five of the six paintings where it covers the most are Japanese or Indian, among them [[painting:cma-133000|Sesshu's splashed-ink landscape]] at 89 per cent, where a pale ground can carry the whole match [10]. The sixth is a frieze by Klimt, [[painting:commons-Q58427233|Yearning for happiness is assuaged in poetry]], at 87 per cent [10].

The rate rises over time, from 6.1 per cent of paintings in the 1600s to 14.3 per cent in the 1900s, and the 1930s peak at 13 of 69 paintings [10]. Impressionism carries it in 28 of 140 works, and [[painter:frederic-remington|Remington]] in 9 of 16 [10]. As always these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a screen color, not a pigment test [10].

The word itself is easy to date. In Google Books, *French grey* rose fastest in the 1810s, the decade of Syme's first edition, and peaked in the 1920s, though the count covers every sense of the phrase [11]. Our archive finds this grey in a painting of 1164, 650 years before the name's earliest record in our sources, a reminder that a color can exist long before its name [10][9].

questions.q: What did Syme say French grey was?
choices: Werner's steel grey without the lustre
Pearl grey with a little blue
questions.answer: Werner's steel grey without the lustre

questions.q: Which natural object did Syme give as his only example of French grey?
choices: The breast of a pied wagtail
The back of a kittiwake gull
questions.answer: The breast of a pied wagtail

questions.q: Why did Darwin carry a color chart on the Beagle?
choices: Sea animals lose their colors quickly once lifted from the water
To match paint for the ship's cabins
questions.answer: Sea animals lose their colors quickly once lifted from the water
